doors.name: The First Loaf
doors.lore: Before the road had mileposts, runners carried a heel of bread to the next oven. The last baker to receive it rang the morning bell.
The underside is covered in pencil strokes. Each spring a child stood here in bare feet. One year the marks begin again at the bottom.

doors.name: The Binding Room
doors.lore: Two hands repaired this book. One used fine thread. The other used fishing line and stitched through the first hand's signature.

doors.name: The Borrowed Wind
doors.lore: The smallest scoop is stamped WIDOW'S SHARE. Grain that fell between the floorboards belonged to the miller. Grain that fell in this scoop never did.

doors.name: The Copper Measure
doors.lore: The crack was plugged with a thumbprint. No bell cast here rings quite cleanly. The guild has rejected three offers to repair the mould.

doors.name: The Chain Dock
doors.lore: Pilots used to braid ribbons through the last link before sailing. A faded yellow knot sits just above the high-water mark.

doors.name: The Cinder Lens
doors.lore: In winter the lens keeper warmed the glass in both hands before polishing it. The cloth in the drawer has two patches worn thin.

doors.name: The Highwater Oven
doors.lore: Before the road had mileposts, runners carried a heel of bread to the next oven. The last baker to receive it rang the morning bell.

doors.name: The Reed School
doors.lore: The pupils learned their letters from ferry wakes. An upright stroke meant a boat was coming home. A loop meant somebody had gone back for another passenger.

doors.name: The Fen Watch
doors.lore: One entry has no hour beside it: a light answered from beneath the water. The keeper trimmed the lamp and answered once.

doors.name: The Linen Ward
doors.lore: A nurse sewed a blue corner onto each bandage washed in boiled water. When the dye ran out, she signed the corners with a single blue stitch.

doors.name: The Drum House
doors.lore: The duty roster calls for two drummers on a fog night. One played. The other listened along the floorboards for the answering beat.

doors.name: The Echo Rotunda
doors.lore: A singer chalked a cross where an echo returned in tune. The floor has been laid three times. Someone always puts the cross back.

doors.name: The Flood Archive
doors.lore: The flooded streets were copied in blue ink. Families returned each spring to write their names in black beside a door they remembered.

doors.name: The Rookery Lodge
doors.lore: Seven notches for crossings in thick fog. An eighth runs the whole length of the shaft. That morning the pilot walked the riverbed home.

doors.name: The Winter Glass
doors.lore: A frost-cracked label reads: White nettle, brought upstairs the night the parish drowned. The handwriting underneath says: It took.

doors.name: The Glasscut Works
doors.lore: The glazier kept one crooked pane from every batch. Look through two together, her notebook says, and a straight road looks like a river.

doors.name: The Gloaming Press
doors.lore: Early editions printed the ferry times in red. A reader wrote beneath the last one: you can hear her oars from my kitchen.

doors.name: Mercy Rest
doors.lore: Boots were dried toe-out for travellers going east and heel-out for those going west. The empty peg was always kept warm.

doors.name: Sounding Toll House
doors.lore: The Sounding stamp is worn smooth on one edge. On flood mornings the clerk turned it sideways. A sideways mark meant the return journey was already paid.

doors.name: Saltwake Toll House
doors.lore: The Saltwake stamp is worn smooth on one edge. In the margin a runner has drawn a cup. The inn across the ridge accepted that mark in place of a coin.

doors.name: Chain Toll House
doors.lore: The Chain stamp is worn smooth on one edge. The debts on this page are in loaves and lamp oil. The column for names has been carefully scraped clean.

doors.name: Kettle Yard Cookhouse
doors.lore: The cook kept the first bowl upside down until the last runner arrived. There is a ring in the table where it stood.

doors.name: The Lantern Court
doors.lore: Each family brought a lamp for the night crossing. One saucer has a saucer-sized patch beneath it where a child scrubbed away the soot every morning.

doors.name: The Linen Exchange
doors.lore: The cloth kept for mending sails has a blue thread along one edge. In the flood, that thread was enough to find the way along a rope in the dark.

doors.name: The Mercy Slip
doors.lore: In the fare book the narrowest ferry is listed as a cradle. A seamstress paid its first crossing with three buttons and a very good needle.

doors.name: The First Loaf
doors.lore: Before the road had mileposts, runners carried a heel of bread to the next oven. The last baker to receive it rang the morning bell.

doors.name: The Thumbprint Kiln
doors.lore: Customers could tell their pots apart by touch. The potter pressed each buyer’s thumb into the clay while the jar was still damp.

doors.name: The Bell & Blanket
doors.lore: Boots were dried toe-out for travellers going east and heel-out for those going west. The empty peg was always kept warm.

doors.name: Spring Chandlery
doors.lore: Every ninth link is brass so a pilot can count it in the dark. The last one is gold. It was once somebody's wedding ring.

doors.name: The Brass Shuttle
doors.lore: In the lean winter a sail was cut into blankets. The weaver kept the blue selvedge and worked an inch of it into every new sail that year.

doors.name: Mossbell Pavilion
doors.lore: One entry has no hour beside it: a light answered from beneath the water. The keeper trimmed the lamp and answered once.

doors.name: The Mould Loft
doors.lore: Three apprentices pressed their initials into the same mould. The middle one wrote backwards so the casting would carry her name the right way round.

doors.name: The Orrery Loft
doors.lore: The smallest wheel runs a little fast. A note by its pin reads: leave it. It keeps my brother’s ferry time.
Six patches of sailcloth, all different blues. The smallest has a mast stitched on backwards. Nobody has unpicked it.
Every wick had a name in this household. A neat line beside Grandmother reads: still burns an hour on a thimble of oil.
A wooden foot with one heel worn flat. Folded inside its stocking is a receipt for two left boots, delivered to two different people.

doors.name: The Paper Playhouse
doors.lore: A child punched two holes in this ticket. One admitted her. The other admitted her shadow, which had a speaking part.

doors.name: The Rain Court
doors.lore: Someone measured a lean summer in cups of rain. Beside the smallest mark is a drawing of a pear, with five names around it.

doors.name: The Lock House
doors.lore: The first pump clattered like a rook. Its makers slipped this shim under the bearing. The village birds kept answering it for another week.

doors.name: The Thawing Post
doors.lore: Boots were dried toe-out for travellers going east and heel-out for those going west. The empty peg was always kept warm.
Inside the lid someone scratched a little boat. Even with the crock full, the boat sits just above the butter.

doors.name: The Kite Loft
doors.lore: In fog the foresters flew paper birds above the branches. A red tail meant the path was open. A white tail meant wait for me.

doors.name: The Saffron Kilns
doors.lore: A potter left a row of thumb bowls for the night shift. Each fits a different hand. One has a hollow for a missing finger.

doors.name: Saltwake Chandlery
doors.lore: Every ninth link is brass so a pilot can count it in the dark. The last one is gold. It was once somebody's wedding ring.

doors.name: The Signal Loom
doors.lore: The first signal cloth was a striped apron. The weavers have saved one of its mother-of-pearl buttons in the shuttle drawer.

doors.name: The Oar House

doors.name: Ada's Chart Office
doors.lore: The stone on Ada's maps came from the old river crossing. Turn it over and the slow green curve of the lost channel is still visible.

doors.name: The Sounding Office
doors.lore: Soundings used to be called out in a singing voice. A pilot has written the deepest channel as four notes along the margin of the chart.

doors.name: The Still Belfry
doors.lore: The bell has two founders’ marks. One belongs to the caster. The other is a child’s palm pressed into the sand before the pour.

doors.name: The Pump Guild
doors.lore: When the pumps stopped, neighbours passed buckets hand to hand. There are still two sets of handles on the smallest bucket.

doors.name: The Common Table
doors.lore: A baker once fed both banks from these steps. Her soup recipe survives, except for the final line: keep adding water until everybody is here.

doors.name: Swallow Pump House
doors.lore: The first pump clattered like a rook. Its makers slipped this shim under the bearing. The village birds kept answering it for another week.

doors.name: The Twin Intake
doors.lore: Two keepers argued over which gate sang lower. Their tally ends with a diagram of two wet boots and the words: both wrong.

doors.name: The Vellum Exchange
doors.lore: Look closely at the parchment offcuts. The mapmaker let children draw imaginary bridges on them. One bridge appears on a later survey.

doors.name: The Public Weigh House
doors.lore: Alongside the iron weights hangs a little bag of buttons. Anyone short a penny could leave one here. The clerk never counted how many were left.

doors.name: The Wick House
doors.lore: The wick cutter measured a winter evening from thumb to elbow. Her left sleeve is embroidered with the short measure for summer.

doors.name: The Pilot's Table
doors.lore: Seven notches for crossings in thick fog. An eighth runs the whole length of the shaft. That morning the pilot walked the riverbed home.

doors.name: The Tide Chapel
doors.lore: Each spring the chapel sent a candle downriver in a little boat. The cupboard holds one boat for every year the river was too rough to launch it.

doors.name: The Last Lamp
doors.lore: One entry has no hour beside it: a light answered from beneath the water. The keeper trimmed the lamp and answered once.
